Notice the moment without making calm another demand.

The idea to keep in mind

Awareness and relaxation are not the same goal.

A practice may help you notice what is happening even when it does not make you feel peaceful. More intense attention is not automatically more helpful.

Understanding the approach

Mindfulness concerns the relationship with experience.

Mindfulness involves attention to present experience with an effort not to immediately judge it. In therapy, it may help a person notice thoughts, sensations, emotions, and reactions before responding automatically. It is not a requirement to stop thinking or to turn a painful event into a positive one.

Mindfulness-based therapy is a broad description. Mindfulness-Based Stress Reduction and Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy are named programs with their own structures; selected mindfulness practices used by an individual clinician are not necessarily either complete program. Ask what is actually being offered.

Research varies across practices, populations, and outcomes. NCCIH notes both possible benefits and limitations in the evidence, as well as the need to take adverse experiences seriously. A practice is not universally harmless because it is quiet, brief, or described as natural.

Sources mindfulness psychotherapy

In plain language

The practice should serve your life.

The purpose might be noticing a reaction earlier or returning attention to an important task. Performing a meditation correctly is not the only meaningful measure of progress.

Go a little deeper

Different practices can have different purposes.

These descriptions explain options a clinician might discuss. They are not instructions to complete an exercise on this page.

01Noticing attentionRecognize when the mind has moved, then choose how to respond.Read more +

Attention naturally shifts. A practice can involve noticing that shift and returning to a chosen point of focus. The return is part of learning, not evidence that the previous moment was a failure.

A clinician should explain why that practice relates to your goal rather than assume that everyone needs the same routine.

02Observing thoughtsTreat a thought as an event to notice, not automatically a fact or command.Read more +

Mindfulness can help distinguish having a thought from acting on it. This is different from proving the thought wrong or suppressing it. Some concerns still need careful evaluation and action.

The approach should not invalidate realistic fear, discrimination, or an unsafe situation by calling it merely a thought.

03Awareness of sensationsWork with bodily experience at a tolerable pace.Read more +

Some practices involve sensations or breathing; others use an external focus or ordinary activity. Inward attention can be uncomfortable or destabilizing for some people.

Discuss alternatives, accessibility needs, and permission to pause. Keeping eyes closed or concentrating on breathing should not be treated as a universal requirement.

04Bringing awareness into daily lifeConnect noticing with what matters outside the exercise.Read more +

A practice may be useful during a transition, a conversation, or another everyday moment. Its value depends on whether it supports participation and choice, not just the number of minutes completed.

Formal programs and informal practices should not be treated as interchangeable when discussing evidence or training.

Sources mindfulness psychotherapy

A worked example

An anxious thought arrives during dinner. Attention can move again.

A fictional example about noticing attention, not a breathing exercise or a treatment plan.

Fictional teaching example. Not a diagnosis, a client story, or an assigned exercise.

01

The interruption

While eating with friends, Rowan remembers an unfinished work task. Their attention moves into a rehearsal of everything that could go wrong.

02

The extra struggle

Rowan then criticizes themselves for being anxious and tries to force the thought away. The effort to control it occupies still more attention.

03

A different relationship

In therapy, Rowan might explore noticing that worry is present and choosing where to place attention next, without requiring the worry to disappear first.

What would count as a useful difference?

A useful difference might be returning to the conversation for a few moments rather than spending the meal arguing internally with worry. That is not proof the concern is unimportant; the work task can be addressed at an appropriate time. Attention practice and practical problem-solving can coexist.

This example should not be treated as an instruction to ignore danger, pain, or significant symptoms. If an inward-focused practice increases panic, disconnection, or distress, the clinician should adapt or stop it and assess what is needed.

Sources mindfulness psychotherapy

Inside the work

A purposeful introduction is better than an unexplained exercise.

01

Clarify the aim

The clinician explains what a practice is intended to support and how it connects with the concern you are bringing.

02

Choose an appropriate form

Discuss comfort, previous experiences, accessibility, and alternatives. A method can be adapted rather than imposed.

03

Notice the actual response

The clinician and client pay attention to whether the experience is useful, neutral, or distressing. There is no need to report calm to make the exercise seem successful.

04

Review its place in care

A practice may be retained, changed, or stopped. It should sit within an appropriate plan rather than replace needed treatment or medical care.

Sources mindfulness psychotherapy

Fit, choice and limitations

Mindfulness is an option, not an obligation.

Benefits are not universal

Studies concern different methods and populations, and their findings cannot be applied equally to every practice. A clinician should discuss the rationale and alternatives without promising a cure or a predictable emotional state.

Discomfort deserves attention

Increased anxiety, low mood, or disconnection should not automatically be dismissed as resistance or a necessary breakthrough. The response should inform whether the practice continues and what support is needed.

Sources mindfulness psychotherapy

Your questions, answered

More to know before choosing.

Do I have to stop thinking?

No. Mindfulness does not require an empty mind. Noticing that thoughts have appeared can be part of the practice. Trying to suppress every thought can become another struggle rather than the intended work.

Is this religious?

Meditative practices have varied historical and cultural roots. Clinical programs may use secular forms. Ask what the clinician proposes and discuss your preferences and boundaries rather than assuming all practices have the same meaning.

What if focusing on breathing makes me anxious?

Tell the clinician. An alternative focus, a different approach, or stopping the practice may be appropriate. This website does not prescribe breathwork or advise pushing through panic.

Is MBCT the same as any mindfulness-based session?

No. Mindfulness-Based Cognitive Therapy is a named program, while a clinician may use selected mindfulness practices in other kinds of therapy. Training, program structure, and evidence should be described specifically.

Can this replace other treatment?

Do not use mindfulness as a reason to postpone needed medical or mental health care. It may be one part of a plan, but the appropriate treatment depends on the person and concern.

How would we evaluate whether it helps?

Use the agreed goal and the actual effect on daily life. Being more able to notice and choose a response can matter even without immediate relaxation. Worsening distress is equally important information.

For practical questions, contact the support team. Please keep clinical details out of the initial email.
